content: Vitamin poisoning, also known as hypervitaminosis, is a medical condition characterized by abnormally high levels of stored vitamins in the body, which can result in toxic symptoms. The specific name of the condition depends on the vitamin involved; for instance, an excess of vitamin A is referred to as hypervitaminosis A. Certain vitamins, particularly those outside the vitamin B complex, may cause side effects when consumed in excessive amounts. These side effects are typically reversible and subside quickly once the intake of the supplement is reduced or discontinued. However, some vitamins do not exhibit toxicity even at very high levels. For example, vitamin C has been administered in doses exceeding 100,000 mg (over 1,000 times the recommended daily intake) for severe illnesses without causing adverse effects. That said, vitamin C is known to have a significant laxative effect, particularly when consumed in amounts ranging from 5 to 20 grams per day in otherwise healthy individuals. High doses of mineral supplements can also lead to side effects and toxicity. Cases of mineral supplement poisoning, such as those involving excessive intake of iron-containing supplements (including certain multivitamins), do occur but are relatively uncommon. The United States Department of Agriculture has established tolerable upper intake levels for most vitamins to help prevent such occurrences. Deaths caused by vitamin poisoning are exceedingly rare in the United States, with typically no fatalities reported in a given year. However, prior to 1998, several deaths annually were linked to pharmaceutical iron-containing supplements, particularly brightly colored, sugar-coated, high-potency iron supplements. Most of these fatalities involved children. Since the implementation of unit packaging restrictions for supplements containing more than 30 mg of iron, the number of deaths has decreased to zero or one per year. For comparison, in 2003, there were 59 deaths attributed to aspirin poisoning, 147 deaths associated with acetaminophen-containing products, and an average of 54 deaths per year caused by lightning strikes between 1990 and 2003.
